Couplet.note: The catalog describes the rhymed, same-meter instance. The broader couplet is a consecutive two-line unit; rhyme and equal meter are not universal.

Heroic couplet.note: Each member of the pair is iambic pentameter. End-stopping and a complete sentence are possible rather than mandatory.

edges.evidence: Both pentameter line endings rhyme in the heroic pair.

Octosyllabic couplet.note: Two successive eight-syllable lines share an end rhyme. The catalog fixes syllable count without specifying every foot.

edges.evidence: Eight syllables per line specialize the rhymed pair.

Hudibrastic verse.note: The comic pair follows the octosyllabic couplet; forced or extended rhymes are a characteristic technique.

edges.evidence: The Hudibrastic comic rhymes occur within octosyllabic pairs.

Alexandrine couplet.note: The catalog's two twelve-syllable lines rhyme. Its medial pause belongs within each line, not between the pair.

edges.evidence: Two alexandrines make the rhymed pair in this entry.

Fourteener.note: A fourteener is one fourteen-syllable line. The catalog supplies a paired setting; breaking each line after eight produces the 8–6–8–6 quatrain.

edges.evidence: Fourteener names a line. In the paired example, two such lines form a rhymed couplet.
Dividing a rhyming pair of fourteeners at 8+6 yields a four-line ballad-meter setting.

Poulter's measure.note: The pair comprises one twelve-syllable line and one fourteen-syllable line with a shared end rhyme. Its members have different lengths.

edges.evidence: Poulter pairs the 12- and 14-syllable lines with one rhyme while alternating their meters.
The second line of each Poulter pair is a fourteen-syllable line.

Elegiac couplet.note: An elegiac distich orders hexameter before pentameter. In the classical model the latter has two matching-length halves separated at a word boundary. The catalog marks rhyme as unusual.

edges.evidence: The elegiac distich is a two-line unit even though its members differ in meter and typically do not rhyme.

Skeltonic verse.note: A run sustains one end rhyme across short irregular lines. The source fixes neither the run length nor a larger stanza.

Tumbling verse.note: The catalog's Tudor example uses loosely measured four-stress rhymed pairs. Exact syllable counts are unspecified.

edges.evidence: This catalog entry explicitly groups its four-stress lines in rhymed pairs.

Leonine verse.note: One end rhyme pairs with the word immediately before the mid-line pause. Both rhyme positions are inside a single line.

Tercet.note: The defining unit has three lines. The source leaves their rhymes and meter open.

Triplet.note: All three ends rhyme AAA. This specifies a monorhymed instance of the general three-line unit.

edges.evidence: The triplet adds one shared rhyme to a three-line stanza.

Sicilian tercet.note: The middle rhyme differs from the two outside rhymes. All three lines are in pentameter.

edges.evidence: The Sicilian tercet sets three pentameter lines to ABA.

Terza rima.note: Each tercet's middle rhyme becomes the next tercet's outside rhyme. Three displayed tercets illustrate the chain; one line or a couplet can close it. The two possible endings share a single closing position.

edges.evidence: ABA, BCB and subsequent links are successive three-line units.
The catalog permits a couplet as an alternative ending to the single line.

Quatrain.note: Four lines define this stanza. The multiple listed rhyme schemes are alternatives.

Ballad stanza.note: The catalog's four alternating four- and three-stress lines rhyme ABCB. A refrain or burden is optional; its precise placement is unspecified.

edges.evidence: Four lines in alternating stress lengths form the ballad stanza.

Common metre (CM).note: The catalog prescribes alternating eight- and six-syllable iambic lines. ABAB and ABCB are alternative rhymings of those same lines.

edges.evidence: Four lines carry the complete 8–6–8–6 unit.

Common metre double (CMD).note: Two complete common-meter quatrains make one eight-line unit. Both halves retain the 8–6–8–6 line lengths.

edges.evidence: One doubled stanza includes two complete common-meter quatrains in succession.

Long metre (LM).note: Four iambic tetrameter lines account for the 8–8–8–8 hymn-meter designation.

edges.evidence: Four iambic tetrameter lines make the single long-meter stanza.

Long metre double (LMD).note: Two long-meter quatrains make one stanza, each preserving all four eight-syllable lines.

edges.evidence: The doubled stanza consists of two long-meter quatrains.

Short metre (SM).note: The alias 6.6.8.6 identifies the four line lengths and explains why the third line is longer.

edges.evidence: The four counts 6–6–8–6 fill one stanza.

Short metre double (SMD).note: Two complete short-meter quatrains each repeat 6–6–8–6.

edges.evidence: Two copies of the four-line short-meter unit make the doubled form.

Hallelujah metre.note: The first four lines are six syllables and alternate ABAB. A pair of eight-syllable C lines closes the six-line unit.

edges.evidence: The catalog's 6.6.6.6.8.8 stanza comprises six lines.
The two final C-rhymed eight-syllable lines form the terminal pair.

Trochaic hymn metres.note: The four alias entries give two count patterns, each in single and doubled forms. The alternatives are not successive sections.

edges.evidence: Each single hymn pattern has four lines; doubled versions repeat the complete four-line unit.

Other named hymn metres.note: The aliases supply seven alternative syllable recipes. A dot separates lines, and D doubles the first four-line recipe.

Heroic quatrain.note: Four pentameter lines alternate ABAB. The name elegiac stanza here denotes this English stanza, distinct from the classical elegiac distich.

edges.evidence: The heroic stanza constrains four pentameter lines to ABAB.

In Memoriam stanza.note: Four tetrameter lines enclose the B pair inside A endings. ABBA describes rhyme and does not itself split the quatrain into separate stanzas.

edges.evidence: Four tetrameter lines carry the In Memoriam stanza's enclosing rhyme.

Rubaiyat stanza.note: The catalog specifies AABA. In the optional linked variant the B of one stanza sets the main rhyme of the next. The optional link belongs to line 3, not to a fifth time slot.

edges.evidence: Each AABA rubaiyat stanza remains a four-line unit when several are linked.

Monorhymed quatrain.note: All four lines use one rhyme; the catalog calls for a new rhyme when another stanza begins. A change of rhyme between stanzas is a relation, not an extra leaf after line four.

edges.evidence: All four lines of an individual quatrain share one rhyme.

Redondilla.note: This row supplies the octosyllabic ABBA redondilla. Its enclosing rhyme is the one used for the two four-line ends of the espinela examined here.

edges.evidence: The named Spanish pattern here comprises four octosyllables in ABBA order.

Sapphic stanza.note: Three eleven-syllable lines followed by a five-syllable Adonic line describe the catalog's ordinary Sapphic stanza. The numbers alone do not specify Aeolic quantity.

edges.evidence: The three longer Sapphics and short Adonic occupy four line positions.

Alcaic stanza.note: The catalog's 11–11–9–10 counts agree with the Alcaic template. Its double dactyl belongs at the start of the last line, not at the line ending.

edges.evidence: The alcaic strophe contains exactly four lines with unequal lengths.

Asclepiad stanza.note: Four Asclepiads are one attested setting. Other arrangements mix Asclepiads and shorter Aeolic lines. The catalog does not identify a single variant for every setting.

edges.evidence: The catalog explicitly treats four-line settings; their individual line types may differ.

Quintain.note: The grouping requires five lines. Its listed rhyme patterns are examples, not mandatory internal divisions.

Sestet / sixain.note: The grouping requires six lines. The catalog gives several possible rhyme schemes.

Venus and Adonis stanza.note: Six pentameter lines have four alternating end rhymes ABAB followed by the rhyming CC pair.

edges.evidence: The four ABAB lines and the two C lines make one six-line stanza.
The fifth and sixth pentameter lines rhyme CC.

Burns stanza.note: AAABAB fixes the six rhyme positions. The fourth and sixth lines are shorter and share B.

edges.evidence: The two short tag lines occupy positions four and six of the six-line stanza.

Tail-rhyme stanza.note: The six-line instance divides into two long rhymed pairs, each followed by a short tail. The tails rhyme with one another.

edges.evidence: Two three-line pair-and-tail groups account for all six lines.
The opening lines of each group are a long rhyming pair.

Rhyme royal.note: Seven pentameter lines rhyme ABABBCC with a closing couplet. The specific seven-line scheme distinguishes it from the catalog's catch-all Septet entry.

edges.evidence: Both entries have seven lines; the catalog reserves its catch-all Septet row for other seven-line patterns.
The two final pentameter lines rhyme CC.

Septet.note: This catalog heading collects other seven-line stanzas. It does not prescribe a meter, rhyme scheme, or seven-line form with priority over the named ones.

Ottava rima.note: The English example comprises six alternating pentameter lines then the closing rhymed pair, ABABABCC. The Italian source tradition uses different line lengths.

edges.evidence: Ottava rima is an eight-line stanza; this link concerns octave, not the specific French huitain rhyme scheme.
The last two lines form a rhymed CC pair after the alternating six.

Sicilian octave.note: An eight-line stanza alternates AB throughout. No further internal division is specified in this row.

edges.evidence: Its eight alternating lines satisfy the octave's line count; they do not use the catalog's narrower huitain scheme.

Rispetto.note: The catalog's ABABCCDD setting has four alternating lines then two rhymed pairs. The row does not establish that setting as the sole possible rispetto.

edges.evidence: The eight lines of the listed rispetto form an octave, without the French huitain's additional requirements.
The ABABCCDD example ends in successive CC and DD rhyme pairs.

Monk's Tale stanza.note: The eight-line ABABBCBC pattern matches the Chaucerian stanza. The octave comparison refers to length; the catalog's stricter huitain variant adds a syllable requirement.

edges.evidence: Its eight lines form an octave; matching the huitain rhyme letters does not establish the same meter.

Octave / huitain.note: An octave groups eight lines. The huitain example adds eight syllables per line and ABABBCBC; those extra properties do not apply to every octave.

Spenserian stanza.note: Eight pentameter lines and one longer alexandrine carry the nine rhyme positions ABABBCBCC. The final alexandrine is one line rather than a pair.

edges.evidence: Both use alexandrine lines. The Spenserian stanza incorporates one, whereas the paired form uses two.

Dizain.note: Ten line endings follow ABABBCCDCD. The row gives no smaller sectional boundaries.

Décima espinela.note: Ten octosyllabic lines rhyme ABBAACCDDC. A documented internal reading is two enclosing-rhyme quatrains joined by two bridge lines. This is one analysis, and décima also names a broader family.

edges.evidence: The documented 4+2+4 reading places ABBA and CDDC redondillas on each side of two bridge lines.

Keatsian ode stanza.note: Keats's Nightingale uses the ten-line template ABABCDECDE. To Autumn has eleven-line stanzas; the ten-line model is an example, not a requirement for Keatsian odes.

edges.evidence: In the ten-line Nightingale example the first four lines form the opening ABAB quatrain.
In the ten-line Nightingale example a six-line CDECDE unit follows the quatrain.

Christ's Kirk stanza.note: The printed Christis Kirk opens its stanzas with eight alternating lines, then a bob and a refrain. The refrain text varies, so the catalog's proposed final words are not obligatory.

Pearl stanza.note: The twelve-line rhyme scheme is secure. In Pearl one section has six stanzas; link words recur in the next opening line without having to be its first word. Editors also differ on how strictly to scan the line.

Cherry and Slae stanza.note: Montgomerie's opening stanzas demonstrate a six-line AABCCB group then alternating DEDE and FGFG. The last four lines alternate short and longer lines. This diagram describes that example.

edges.evidence: The first two and fourth and fifth lines rhyme in pairs in the printed Montgomerie example.

Bob and wheel.note: The long alliterative passage leads into a short bob and a four-line wheel. The bob contributes the first A of the five-line ABABA closing group.

edges.evidence: The four-line wheel follows the bob and completes the five-line rhyme group.

Horatian ode.note: The recurring unit is a short stanza of the same design. The source supplies neither a stanza count nor one required internal meter.

Blank verse.note: The catalog's English pattern consists of unrhymed iambic pentameter lines. Grouping into verse paragraphs is one layout; dramatic dialogue also uses blank verse.

Alliterative verse.note: The catalog specifies the Old English type: two half-lines linked by alliteration across the break. It supplies no fixed stanza length.

Accentual verse.note: A fixed count of main stresses permits unstressed material to vary. The source's alias dolnik needs qualification: Russian dolnik trimeter specifically constrains the intervals between accents.

Sprung rhythm.note: Hopkins counts feet beginning in one stress; successive stresses can touch, and weak syllables can follow. He also describes exceptions to the usual one-to-four-syllable foot.

edges.evidence: Both count stresses. Hopkins also gives specific foot shapes and exceptional licenses for sprung rhythm.

Syllabic verse.note: Syllables determine the line measurement. Any recurring sequence of line lengths is specific to the poem, not required by the general category.

Accentual hexameter.note: The English meter counts six stresses in a largely dactylic line. Six groups each containing exactly three syllables would overstate the rule.

edges.evidence: Its organizing count is six metrical stresses; an unstressed syllable total alone does not set the line.

Quantitative verse.note: Here syllable length distinguishes long from short. A chosen metrical scheme arranges them; the umbrella term has no single fixed sequence.

Hendecasyllabics.note: The source specifically names Catullan, unrhymed eleven-syllable lines. The row's syllable total alone does not specify a complete Phalaecian quantity pattern.

Galliambic.note: The central division and two spans of a fast many-syllable line are supported. The catalog gives no complete quantitative formula for its cited English imitation.

Anacreontic verse.note: The catalog's example uses a rhyming pair of seven-syllable lines. Themes of wine and love describe subject matter, not additional sections.

edges.evidence: The seven-syllable lines in this catalog example are grouped in rhymed pairs.
